claim: A two-state solution is still on the table and only Israel blocks it.

answer: The claim is half right. Israel's Knesset voted 68 to 9 in July 2024 against a Palestinian state west of the Jordan, and in September 2025 Prime Minister Netanyahu said there will be none, so Israel's government is not offering one. But Israel is not the only obstacle. Hamas's 2017 document accepts a state on the 1967 lines only as a stage, without recognising Israel or giving up armed struggle, and the Palestinian Authority, which has pledged to disarm Hamas and hold elections, lost Gaza to Hamas in 2007. Many countries recognised Palestine in 2024-25 and 142 states backed the UN's two-state declaration, yet Gallup finds only 26 percent of Israelis and 32 percent of West Bank Palestinians support two states. Our reading: two states remain the declared goal of the Palestinian Authority and most of the world, but neither the Israeli government nor Hamas accepts it.

contested: Whether a two-state outcome is still physically possible. The case that it is not: Avi Shlaim wrote in 2013 that settlement expansion had shrunk the area available for a Palestinian state 'to the point where a two-state solution is barely conceivable', Canada's prime minister cites 'unrelenting' settlement expansion, and in the PCPSR's 2018 poll 56 percent of Palestinians already said settlements had expanded too much for the solution to be viable. The case that it is: Peace Now counts about 14 percent of West Bank residents as settlers (2019), the Clinton Parameters in 2000 would have let Israel keep blocs holding about 80 percent of settlers, and Olmert's 2008 map annexed 4.9 percent of the West Bank (both on the other card); Israel removed about 8,000 settlers from Gaza in 2005. Peace Now also reports that in 2018 more than half of settler population growth was in settlements Israel would probably have to evacuate under the Geneva Initiative's border, which cuts the other way. The card does not choose.

Whether Palestinian leaders can deliver security. The case that they cannot: Hamas won the 2006 election and took Gaza by force in 2007, Hamas's 2017 document keeps armed struggle and non-recognition, and the Knesset resolution argues that 'it will only be a matter of a short time until Hamas takes over' a Palestinian state. The case that they can: Abbas's June 2025 letter commits to disarming Hamas, inviting Arab and international forces and holding elections, France called the pledges unprecedented, and Canada and Australia tied their recognition to such commitments. Whether the pledges will be kept is untested; the PA lost Gaza once and its own president is, by PCPSR's October 2025 summary, unpopular (a PDF we could only read in part).

What the 2024 Knesset vote means. Supporters say it states what Israelis conclude from 7 October and from Gaza after 2005; critics, including Barghouti, call it the end of Oslo. It was non-binding, and two Israeli opposition parties declined to vote for it. The February 2024 Knesset resolution, which the Times of Israel says opposed only unilateral recognition and left room for negotiated statehood, is not on this card because we could not read a page that quotes it.

Whether recognition helps. Macron and the New York Declaration present it as keeping the option alive; Netanyahu and Lapid call it a 'prize' or 'reward' for terror; the UN General Assembly declaration itself condemns Hamas.

Polls differ by pollster and by whether Gaza is included. Gallup and Pew did not poll Gaza after the war began; the Palestinian Center for Policy and Survey Research polls the West Bank and Gaza and generally finds higher support, with Gaza above the West Bank; its detailed 2025 figures are in PDFs we could not read.
could_not_verify: Anything after November 2025. The Israeli government's current position after the 2026 election cycle, any change in the PA's election plans, and the status of Resolution 2803 in 2026 were not verified; the card reflects statements through November 2025.
The text of Hamas's 2017 document itself: we rely on the Guardian, BBC and CFR. The 1988 charter's text and Hamas statements since 7 October 2023 on a state were not read.

The Times of Israel, Reuters and AP pages on the Knesset vote and the UN vote would not load; the UN press release listing the September 2025 recognitions would not load; the Saudi-French joint statement would not load.

Fewer than three reliable sources: the Netanyahu statement (two news pages plus an Israeli government page), the PA's letter (two news pages plus a Canadian government page), the 2024 recognitions (two news pages), the UN General Assembly vote (UN News and the Guardian), Resolution 2803 (the UN and NBC).

Which countries recognise Palestine today: the Guardian's count of 147 UN states in September 2025 is before the wave of recognitions that day; we did not find a reliable page giving the post-September total.
The Palestinian Authority's stated position on Israel's right to exist and on payments to prisoners' families: not read, so not stated.
A reliable HTML page for PCPSR's October 2025 poll and the Pulse polls of 2020-2022: PDF only. The PCPSR listing page is cited for one sentence.
not_claimed: Listing who said no to what does not by itself assign blame: a government can refuse for security reasons, domestic politics, or principle, and the card does not rank the refusals.
It does not claim recognition by other countries creates a state, or that the Knesset resolution is law.
It does not claim all Israelis oppose a Palestinian state, or all Palestinians support one; the polls show most on both sides do not currently support the two-state concept.
It does not claim Hamas accepts two states: its 2017 document accepts a state on the 1967 lines as a stage, without recognising Israel.
It does not claim the PA's 2025 pledges have been carried out.
